stem: Your support agent progressively summarizes the conversation every 10 turns to control token growth. On billing disputes that run past turn 30, transcripts show the agent quoting a refund of "around $350" when the amount agreed at turn 8 was $347.82, and describing the promised delivery date as "early next week" when the customer had been told 12 March. The summaries themselves read as accurate prose. What change most directly prevents this?

options.text: Increase the summarization interval from every 10 turns to every 25 turns, so fewer compression passes run over the same figures.
Keep the last 20 turns verbatim and summarize only what falls outside that window, so recent commitments are never compressed.
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers) into a persistent case facts block included in every request, outside the summarized history.
Instruct the summarizer in its prompt to always preserve numbers, dates and stated commitments verbatim when it condenses the history, and to flag any it cannot fit in.

explanation: Progressive summarization is doing exactly what it was asked to do: condensing. The fix is to keep the facts that must survive verbatim out of the stream being condensed, in a case facts block regenerated into each prompt.

why.A: Delays the loss rather than preventing it, and long disputes still cross the interval several times.
why.B: The $347.82 was agreed at turn 8, so past turn 30 it sits outside the 20-turn window and is compressed anyway.
why.D: A prompt instruction against a compression step is probabilistic, and the failures already cost money when they occur.

stem: Each lookup_order call returns 43 fields, including full shipping event history, warehouse codes and carrier metadata. A typical returns conversation makes six lookups, each against a different order. Instrumentation shows raw order payloads occupy 61% of the context window by turn 20, while the agent only ever reasons about order date, item, price, delivery status and return window. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook that trims each lookup_order result to the five relevant fields before it enters context.
Trigger a summarization pass once context usage exceeds 70%, which will compress the accumulated order payloads.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to ignore fields that are not relevant to the current request.
Cache lookup_order responses so a repeat lookup of the same order reuses the earlier result instead of appending the payload again.

explanation: Verbose tool output should be trimmed before it accumulates, not cleaned up afterwards. A PostToolUse hook does this deterministically and for free, at the point where the result enters context.

why.B: Reactive: the tokens were already spent, and summarization now threatens the five fields that actually matter.
why.C: Ignoring a field costs exactly as many tokens as reading it, because the payload is already in the window.
why.D: A returns conversation looks up different orders, so deduplication saves little, and the first copy of each 43-field payload is the bulk of the cost.

stem: Your coordinator concatenates nine subagent reports into a single 58,000-token prompt for the synthesis subagent. Across 30 runs, the final report consistently reflects the first two and the last two reports in the concatenation, while findings from reports 4 through 6 are absent from the output even though they appear verbatim in the input. Reordering the reports moves which findings go missing. What change addresses this?

options.text: Re-run the document analysis subagent for the subtopics covered by reports 4 through 6, since their findings are not reaching synthesis.
Move the synthesis subagent to a model with a larger context window so all nine reports receive adequate attention.
Add an instruction to the synthesis prompt telling the agent to read every section carefully and account for all nine reports.
Place a key findings summary at the start of the aggregated input and organise the full reports below it under explicit section headers.

explanation: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect: material at the beginning and end of a long input is processed reliably, material in the middle is not. Front-loading a key findings summary and marking sections with explicit headers mitigates the position effect without changing the content.

why.A: Blames a subagent that produced correct findings which are demonstrably present in the input.
why.B: The input already fits comfortably; the failure is positional, not a capacity limit.
why.C: An instruction does not change where in a long input the model attends most reliably.

stem: To cut token spend, your team changed each API request to send only the last three turns plus the case facts block instead of the full conversation. Token cost fell 44%. Within a week, quality reports show the agent re-asking for the order number the customer gave six turns earlier, and contradicting a goodwill credit it had offered on the same call. What should you do?

options.text: Expand the case facts block so that it also records every question already asked and every commitment already made over the course of the call.
Restore passing the full conversation history on each request, with the case facts block as a supplement to it rather than a replacement.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent never to repeat a question the customer has already answered.
Widen the window from three turns to twelve turns, since that span covers all of the failures observed so far.

explanation: Conversational coherence depends on the model seeing the actual exchange. The case facts block exists to protect specific values from summarization, not to stand in for the history.

why.A: Grows without bound and reimplements the transcript badly, since coherence depends on wording and sequence, not just a list of facts.
why.C: The agent cannot avoid repeating a question it can no longer see.
why.D: An arbitrary window reproduces the same failure a few turns further out.

stem: The web search subagent returns roughly 12,000 tokens per source: full page text plus its own reasoning about why the page is relevant. The synthesis subagent has a 30,000-token input budget, is exhausted after two sources out of twelve, and produces a report that cites nothing beyond those two, attributing both to "an industry analysis" with no URL or date because the source details sit inside the subagent's prose. Which two changes address this? (Select 2)

options.text: Return structured key facts with relevance scores instead of full page text and reasoning chains.
Have the coordinator truncate every search result to its first 2,000 tokens before forwarding it to synthesis.
Include source metadata (URL, document title, publication date, section location) as structured fields alongside each fact.
Give the synthesis subagent the web search tool so it can fetch the full pages itself whenever it needs more detail.

explanation: When a downstream agent has a tight context budget, upstream agents should return structured key facts and citations rather than verbose content and reasoning. Carrying metadata as structured fields keeps attribution intact at a fraction of the token cost.

why.B: A blunt cut keeps whatever happens to be at the top of a page and discards facts and citations regardless of relevance.
why.D: Over-provisions a specialist with off-role tools and pushes the same volume of page text back into the budget that is already exhausted.

stem: A customer raises three issues in one session: a damaged item on order 88214 worth $89.99, a duplicate charge of $42.50 dated 4 April, and a subscription cancellation. Forty turns in, the agent processes a refund of $42.50 against order 88214 and tells the customer the damaged item is resolved. Reviewing the transcript, the two amounts and their owning issues were correct at turn 9 and blurred together by turn 30. What is the right structural fix?

options.text: Add an interception hook that blocks process_refund whenever the amount does not match any order that has been mentioned in the conversation so far.
Maintain a structured context layer holding one record per issue (issue ID, order ID, amount, status) and regenerate it into every request.
Instruct the agent to re-read the whole conversation before every refund to reconfirm which amount belongs to which issue.
Have the agent handle one issue at a time and decline to open the second until the first is closed.

explanation: Multi-issue sessions need issue-scoped facts persisted outside the summarized narrative, so each order ID, amount and status stays bound to its own issue no matter how long the conversation runs.

why.A: Catches one symptom at the final step while the conflated state still drives everything else the agent says and promises.
why.C: By turn 30 the transcript the agent sees is the summarized version, so re-reading reproduces the same conflation.
why.D: Refuses a legitimate multi-concern request and pushes the sequencing burden onto the customer.

stem: Transcript review finds the following pattern in 22% of escalated cases. The customer writes "please just put me through to a person", the agent replies "let me take a quick look at that for you first", makes four tool calls over 90 seconds, then escalates anyway. Post-contact survey scores for these cases average 2.1 out of 5. What should the agent do when a customer explicitly asks for a human?

options.text: Complete the investigation first so the human agent receives a fully diagnosed case, then escalate with all of the tool findings attached.
Ask the customer whether they would like the agent to attempt a resolution first before being transferred.
Escalate immediately only when sentiment analysis of the message confirms frustration above a configured threshold.
Honour the request immediately by calling escalate_to_human with a structured handoff summary, without first attempting investigation.

explanation: An explicit request for a human is one of the legitimate escalation triggers and is honoured immediately. The handoff summary is what the human needs, and it can be compiled from what is already known.

why.A: Overrides a clearly stated customer preference, which is precisely what the survey scores are punishing.
why.B: Re-litigates a request that left nothing to clarify, adding a turn before the transfer.
why.C: Sentiment is an unreliable proxy and irrelevant here, because the request itself was unambiguous.

stem: A customer writes: "This is the third time I have had to chase this. Your system is a joke." The attached case is a damaged-item replacement with photo evidence, squarely inside the returns policy and fully within the agent's tool capability. The agent currently escalates every message of this tone, and cases like this account for 14% of escalations against an 80% first-contact resolution target. What is the correct behaviour?

options.text: Acknowledge the repeated contact, offer to process the replacement now since it is within policy, and escalate only if the customer then asks for a human.
Process the replacement straight away without responding to the complaint itself, on the basis that a fast resolution speaks louder than an apology does here.
Have the agent self-report a confidence score for each turn and escalate whenever that score falls below 7 out of 10.
Escalate immediately, since three prior contacts and strongly negative wording indicate a case that needs human judgement.

explanation: Frustration is not a complexity signal. When the issue is straightforward and inside the agent's capability, acknowledging the experience and offering resolution is correct, with escalation reserved for the customer restating a preference for a human.

why.B: Ignores a stated service failure, which commonly produces a fourth contact rather than a closed case.
why.C: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and the agent is confident on this easy case, so the score routes nothing.
why.D: Treats sentiment as a proxy for case complexity, which it is not, and spends an escalation on a policy-covered replacement.

stem: A customer asks you to match a competitor's advertised price on an item they bought four days ago. Your written policy covers price adjustments only for items whose price drops on your own site within 14 days of purchase, and says nothing at all about competitor pricing. The agent currently denies these requests by citing the 14-day own-site rule, and 60% of those denials generate a follow-up complaint that a human then approves. What should the agent do?

options.text: Deny the request and explain the 14-day own-site rule, on the basis that anything written policy does not permit is not permitted.
Ask the customer to submit a written appeal to the policy team, and close the contact once they have the appeal reference.
Escalate to a human, because the policy is silent on competitor price matching rather than prohibiting it.
Approve the match when the purchase falls inside the 14-day window, applying the closest analogous rule.

explanation: Policy gaps and ambiguity are a legitimate escalation trigger. A request the policy does not address is a decision the agent has no authority to make in either direction.

why.A: Treats silence as prohibition, which is itself a policy decision, and the human approvals show it is the wrong one.
why.B: Shifts the burden onto the customer when escalate_to_human exists precisely for this case.
why.D: Invents policy by analogy from a rule written for a different situation.

stem: get_customer called with "J. Martinez" returns three matching accounts. The agent currently proceeds with whichever account has the most recent order activity. Over one quarter this produced nine refunds issued against the wrong account, each requiring manual reversal. What instruction should the system prompt carry?

options.text: Escalate the contact to a human agent whenever a customer lookup returns more than one matching account.
Rank the matches by recency of order activity and proceed with the top match, stating clearly in the response which account has been selected.
When a lookup returns more than one match, ask the customer for another identifier such as an order number or postcode before proceeding.
Change get_customer so it returns only its highest-scoring match, keeping the ambiguity from ever reaching the agent.

explanation: Multiple matches are an ambiguity to resolve with the customer, not to guess at. Asking for one more identifier is a single turn and removes the wrong-account risk entirely.

why.A: Disproportionate: one clarifying question resolves nearly all of these, and escalation is reserved for its own triggers.
why.B: Still a heuristic, and stating the selected account in the reply does not make a wrong selection right.
why.D: Hides the ambiguity inside the tool, leaving the same risk while removing the information the agent needs to ask a question.

stem: An audit of 300 transcripts shows escalate_to_human fired 41 times: 18 on strongly worded messages the agent could have resolved itself, 12 after the agent rated its own confidence below its threshold, and 11 on requests no written policy addressed. You are rewriting the escalation criteria block in the system prompt. Which two conditions belong in it? (Select 2)

options.text: The customer's message contains strongly negative language, profanity, or repeated complaints about the service.
The customer's request falls into a gap where written policy is silent or ambiguous.
The agent's self-rated confidence in its proposed resolution is below 7 out of 10 on the scale set in the prompt.
The agent has used the tools available to it and cannot make meaningful progress on the request.

explanation: The legitimate triggers are an explicit request for a human, a policy exception or gap, and an inability to make meaningful progress. Complexity alone is not one, and neither is discomfort.

why.A: Sentiment does not correlate with case complexity, which is what escalation is meant to sort on.
why.C: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so the agent stays confident on exactly the cases it gets wrong.

stem: Your document analysis subagent returns {"results": [], "status": "ok"} in two different situations: when the document store genuinely holds no matching papers, and when the store connection times out. Last week the store was unreachable for 40 seconds during a run, and the published report states "no peer-reviewed evidence was found on regulatory impact". What should change in the subagent's return contract?

options.text: Have the subagent raise an exception that terminates the whole research run whenever the document store is unreachable.
Return an access failure result carrying the failure type, the query attempted and any partial results, distinct from a zero-match success.
Have the subagent retry with exponential backoff and, if the store is still down after that, return the same empty success so the run is not blocked.
Have the coordinator retry every empty result once, on the assumption that some of them are hidden failures.

explanation: An access failure and a valid empty result are different facts and must be reported differently, because the coordinator's correct response to each is different. A zero-match query succeeded; a timeout did not.

why.A: Terminates a whole workflow on one failure when partial results plus a coverage note would still deliver value.
why.C: Silently suppresses the failure, which is what produced the confidently incomplete report in the first place.
why.D: Spends calls re-running genuine zero-match queries and still leaves the coordinator unable to tell the two cases apart.

stem: Your web search subagent propagates every failure to the coordinator, including transient 503 responses from the search API that succeed on a second attempt roughly 80% of the time. The coordinator's only recovery move is to re-delegate the whole search phase, discarding the sources already gathered. Runs that hit a single 503 take three times as long. How should failure handling be split?

options.text: Have the subagent swallow transient errors and simply return whatever results it did manage to gather, with no error field set on the response.
Have the coordinator retry the failed subagent invocation from scratch rather than re-delegating the whole phase.
Add a shared retry service in front of every subagent that transparently retries any failed tool call up to five times.
Have the subagent retry transient failures itself and propagate only what it cannot resolve, with the query attempted and any partial results.

explanation: Transient failures belong to the agent that can see them and retry cheaply. Only what the subagent cannot resolve should reach the coordinator, and it should arrive with what was attempted and what was salvaged.

why.A: Removes the coordinator's ability to tell a thin result from a degraded one, which is the silent suppression anti-pattern.
why.B: Still throws away partial work and re-pays for it, with the coordinator knowing less about the failure than the subagent did.
why.C: Retries non-retryable failures alongside transient ones and still returns nothing structured about what actually happened.

stem: A run covering five subtopics completes with three fully sourced and two returning nothing, because the journal archive holding the relevant literature was behind a paywall the loader could not pass. The coordinator proceeds and the synthesis output reads as an even, confident treatment of all five subtopics with no indication that two were unsupported. What should the synthesis output do instead?

options.text: Carry coverage annotations marking which findings are well supported and which topics have gaps because sources were unavailable.
Drop the two unsupported subtopics from the report scope entirely, so that nothing published rests on missing evidence.
Append a standard disclaimer to the report noting that some sources may not have been reachable during research.
Have the coordinator re-run the research pass until every one of the five subtopics returns at least one source.

explanation: Partial results are worth publishing as long as the reader can tell which parts rest on evidence. Coverage annotations make the gap itself a reported finding rather than an invisible one.

why.B: Hides a known gap from the reader, when the absence of accessible literature is information they need.
why.C: A blanket disclaimer does not tell the reader which specific claims are affected.
why.D: The paywalled archive will not become reachable on retry, so the loop has no terminating condition.

stem: Whenever anything goes wrong, your web search subagent returns the string "search unavailable". The coordinator's only possible recovery is therefore to re-issue the identical request. Logs show 30% of these re-issues fail again for the same underlying reason, a malformed date filter in the generated query, while the rest were transient provider outages that clear on the second attempt. Both defects were found only when an engineer read the subagent's own logs by hand, and they are the third and fourth distinct failure causes found that way this quarter. What should you change first?

options.text: Return a typed failure class plus the query that was sent, so the coordinator can repair a malformed filter and retry an outage.
Raise the coordinator's retry limit for search failures from one to five, so transient outages clear before a run gives up.
Validate the generated date filters inside the subagent before the query is sent, so malformed queries stop reaching the provider.
Have the coordinator prompt the model to infer the likely failure cause from the request it issued before choosing a recovery.

explanation: One status string collapses two failures that need opposite recoveries. Naming the failure class and echoing the query lets the coordinator rewrite a bad filter and simply retry an outage, instead of re-issuing the same request blindly.

why.B: Re-issues the malformed query four more times, since that failure is not transient, and the coordinator still cannot tell which case it is in.
why.C: Fixes the one defect now known while leaving the coordinator blind to the next one, which is what made this one take a manual log read to find.
why.D: Substitutes inference for information the subagent already had and chose not to report.

stem: Your document analysis subagent hits its 15-minute time budget after successfully analysing 7 of the 12 assigned papers. The coordinator must now choose between re-delegating the remainder, proceeding with what it has, and annotating a coverage gap. Which two elements must the subagent's response carry to make that choice possible? (Select 2)

options.text: The seven completed paper analyses, returned as partial results.
The subagent's full reasoning trace for each of the seven papers it did analyse.
The elapsed time each completed analysis took, so the coordinator can size the next budget.
The failure type and the identities of the five papers that were not analysed.

explanation: Structured error context is failure type, what was attempted, what was salvaged and what alternatives exist. Partial results plus a precise statement of what is missing is exactly enough for the coordinator to decide.

why.B: Verbose reasoning consumes the coordinator's context without informing the recovery decision.
why.C: Timing helps tune a budget but says nothing about what is missing or what was salvaged.

stem: Ninety minutes and about 200 tool calls into exploring a 400,000-line legacy Java service, an engineer asks how payments are settled. The agent answers that "the payment flow typically uses a service layer over a repository pattern", although 40 minutes earlier it had read and correctly described PaymentOrchestrator and LegacyGatewayAdapter. It also gives a different answer to the same question asked twice. What is happening and what fixes it?

options.text: The earlier reads have aged out of the context window. Reload every file the agent has read so far at the start of every new question in order to restore them.
The model cannot handle a codebase of this size. Move the exploration agent onto a stronger model with better long-session recall.
This is context degradation in an extended session. Have the agent record key findings to a scratchpad file and read from it on later questions.
The question was underspecified. Re-ask it with an instruction to be specific and to cite a file path for every claim it makes.

explanation: Falling back on generic patterns instead of the specific classes discovered earlier, plus inconsistent answers to the same question, is the signature of context degradation. A scratchpad file persists findings across context boundaries.

why.A: Re-consumes the very budget that caused the degradation, and grows every time it is repeated.
why.B: Reads a context management problem as a model quality problem; a stronger model degrades the same way in a session this long.
why.D: Asks for specificity the model can no longer source, since the material it would cite is no longer available to it.

stem: Your codebase exploration agent must hold a running architectural picture of an unfamiliar repository while answering specific questions like "where are all the integration tests" and "what depends on the refund flow". Each such question produces thousands of lines of Grep hits and file contents, and instrumentation shows raw tool output occupies 70% of the main session's context within 20 minutes. What is the right structure?

options.text: Ask the engineers to identify and paste in only the files they believe are relevant to each question.
Spawn a subagent per investigative question that returns only a summary, keeping verbose discovery output out of the main session.
Have the main agent summarize its own tool output immediately after each search completes and then discard the raw text from its context.
Run /compact whenever context passes 70%, so the session keeps making room for new discovery output.

explanation: Subagent delegation isolates verbose exploration in a context the main session never pays for, returning only the summary the coordinator needs. That preserves the main agent's high-level understanding across many questions.

why.A: Shifts the exploration work back onto the engineers, which is the problem the agent exists to solve.
why.C: The raw output has already entered the main context before any summary of it can be produced.
why.D: Compaction condenses the architectural map the main agent has to keep, and the raw output has already been paid for by the time it runs.

stem: A three-phase migration audit runs as follows. Phase 1 maps module boundaries and fills the coordinator with 60,000 tokens of discovery output. Phase 2 spawns six subagents, one per module. Traces show each phase 2 subagent spends its first 40 minutes re-deriving the same module boundaries phase 1 already established. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Run all three phases in a single session so that nothing discovered in one phase is lost to the next.
Have each phase 2 subagent re-derive the module boundaries itself but on a cheaper model, so the duplicated work costs less.
Rely on the phase 2 subagents inheriting the coordinator's conversation history so they start with the phase 1 discovery already in context.
Summarize the phase 1 key findings and inject that summary into the initial context of each phase 2 subagent.

explanation: Subagents inherit nothing, so whatever phase 2 needs must be handed to it explicitly. Summarizing the phase 1 findings first keeps that handoff small enough to leave each subagent room to work.

why.A: One session accumulates all three phases of verbose output, which is the context exhaustion the phasing exists to prevent.
why.B: Keeps 40 minutes of duplicated work per agent and buys only a discount on it.
why.C: Subagents do not automatically inherit parent context, and 60,000 tokens of raw discovery would exhaust their budgets even if they did.

stem: A four-hour dependency audit fanned out across 12 subagents crashed at the three-hour mark when the build machine restarted. Nine subagents had completed and reported back, but the coordinator's context had been compacted twice by then, so their findings survive in its history only as summary prose. Restarting the audit reruns all twelve from zero. How should you design recovery so a restart resumes rather than repeats?

options.text: Use --resume with a named session so the coordinator continues the crashed conversation where it left off.
Checkpoint the coordinator's full conversation to disk every five minutes and replay the saved transcript into a new session after a crash.
Reduce the audit to four subagents so that rerunning everything after a crash costs proportionally less.
Have each subagent export its completed state to a known location, and have the coordinator load a manifest of those exports on resume.

explanation: Crash recovery in a fan-out design needs durable, structured state per agent plus a manifest the coordinator reads on resume. The nine completed audits then come back as data rather than as work to redo.

why.A: Resumption restores the coordinator's conversation, in which two compaction passes have already blurred the nine completed audits into prose rather than usable findings.
why.B: Replaying three hours of transcript restores tokens rather than queryable state, and the compacted history it replays no longer carries the nine audits in full.
why.C: Accepts the loss and makes it cheaper instead of designing recovery.

stem: Two hours into exploring an unfamiliar 300-file service, context sits at 88% and is dominated by raw Grep and Read output from searches whose conclusions the engineer has already drawn. She wants to keep working in the same session without losing the architectural map built so far: module boundaries, entry points and the six classes that matter. What should the agent do?

options.text: Write the architectural findings to a scratchpad file, then run /compact so the session continues without the raw discovery output.
Record the six key classes and their file paths in the project's CLAUDE.md so they are loaded into every session from now on.
Run /compact immediately, since compaction keeps a summary of the session and drops only the raw tool output.
Start a fresh session and re-explore the service from the beginning, accepting the rework in exchange for a clean context.

explanation: Compaction is a summarization step, and specific class and path names are exactly what summarization tends to blur. Persisting them to a scratchpad first makes the compaction safe.

why.B: Persists the map but leaves the session at 88%, and project instructions are the wrong home for one audit's transient findings.
why.C: Compaction condenses, so the specific class and path names discovered over two hours are the details most at risk if they exist nowhere else.
why.D: Discards two hours of exploration that a scratchpad plus compaction would preserve.

stem: Your extraction pipeline reports 97.2% field-level accuracy across 40,000 documents, and the business wants to remove human review entirely to save reviewer cost. The document mix includes typed invoices, purchase orders, and a small stream of scanned handwritten delivery notes that make up 3% of volume. What must you do before reducing review?

options.text: Recompute the aggregate over a much larger sample, 200,000 documents rather than 40,000, to confirm that the 97.2% figure is genuinely stable.
Reduce review to a flat 5% random sample of all extractions and keep watching the aggregate accuracy figure.
Analyse accuracy segmented by document type and by field, and confirm every segment meets the bar rather than relying on the aggregate.
Keep human review only for extractions where the model reports low confidence, and automate the rest.

explanation: An aggregate of 97.2% is compatible with a document type at 60% when that type is 3% of volume. Segmenting by document type and field is what exposes a weak segment before it is automated away.

why.A: More data on the same aggregate is still the same aggregate, and it hides the same segment.
why.B: A flat sample of a skewed population still buries a small weak document type inside the same aggregate.
why.D: Confidence routing is only safe once accuracy has been checked segment by segment, and a weak 3% stream can be extracted confidently and wrongly.

stem: Human review currently re-checks only the 8% of extractions the model flags below its confidence threshold. Reviewers have surfaced no new error classes in six months. A downstream finance team then reports that invoices from one vendor family have been arriving with the currency symbol captured inside the numeric amount field for most of that period, every one of them extracted at confidence 0.95 or above. What should you add to the review workflow?

options.text: Add a validation rule that rejects any amount field containing a non-numeric character and returns that document for re-extraction automatically.
Ongoing stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, to measure the true error rate and surface novel error patterns.
Lower the confidence threshold so that a larger share of extractions is routed into the existing review queue.
Have reviewers re-check every extraction for one month to establish a full picture of the error landscape.

explanation: Sampling only what the model already doubts can never find errors hiding in the confident pile. Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions is what makes novel error patterns visible.

why.A: Fixes the one symptom now known and leaves the detection gap that let it run unnoticed for six months.
why.C: Adds volume to the band already under review, while these failures sit at 0.95, far above any workable threshold.
why.D: Unaffordable and one-off, producing a snapshot rather than ongoing measurement.

stem: Your extractor emits a single confidence value per document and the review threshold was set at 0.8 by judgement. A retrospective against 2,000 labelled documents shows that within the 0.85 to 0.90 band, the vendor_tax_id field is wrong 11% of the time while invoice_date is wrong 0.6% of the time. Reviewer capacity is fixed. How should review routing be redesigned?

options.text: Abandon confidence routing and review a fixed 20% random sample of all documents, spending the fixed capacity uniformly.
Have the model emit confidence per field, then calibrate a review threshold for each field against the labelled set.
Instruct the model to report lower confidence on identifier fields, since those are where the errors concentrate.
Raise the global threshold from 0.8 to 0.95, so everything in the 0.85 to 0.90 band reaches a reviewer.

explanation: Error rates differ by an order of magnitude between fields, so a single document-level score cannot route attention well. Field-level confidence calibrated on labelled data puts fixed reviewer capacity where the errors actually are.

why.A: Spends the same capacity uniformly and ignores the very difference the retrospective revealed.
why.C: An uncalibrated instruction shifts the numbers without making them mean anything measurable.
why.D: Floods the queue with invoice_date extractions that are almost always right, while capacity stays fixed.

stem: About 3% of your scanned purchase orders carry two different totals: a printed figure and a handwritten correction beside it. The extractor picks one, reports confidence above 0.9, and is wrong roughly half the time. Daily volume is 9,000 documents and reviewer capacity is 400. How should these documents be handled?

options.text: Re-run the extraction on the same document three times and take the value returned by the majority of attempts.
Add a prompt rule instructing the model to always prefer the handwritten correction over the printed figure.
Have the extractor flag contradictory source values explicitly and route only those documents to human review.
Route the 400 lowest-confidence documents to review each day, whatever their document type.

explanation: Ambiguous or contradictory source documents are exactly what limited human review capacity should be spent on. Detecting the conflict and routing it beats guessing at it confidently.

why.A: The ambiguity lives in the source, not in the extraction, so repeated attempts cannot settle what the document leaves open.
why.B: Invents a business rule the documents do not support, since the printed figure is sometimes the corrected one.
why.D: These documents are extracted above 0.9 confidence, so they never enter a lowest-confidence queue.

stem: The document analysis subagent returns prose summaries with inline citations such as "(Okonkwo 2024, p. 17)". The synthesis subagent compresses 40 such summaries into 12 paragraphs. Spot-checking the published report, 60% of citations either point to the wrong paper or have disappeared, although the analysis subagent's own output was correct. What is the right fix?

options.text: Have subagents emit claim-source mappings (claim, excerpt, document, page) as structured fields that synthesis carries through.
Have the report generator re-search the source pool for a matching citation for each claim after synthesis, and attach whichever match scores highest for it.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to carefully preserve every inline citation when it condenses the summaries.
Have the synthesis subagent produce longer output so there is more room for the citations to survive compression.

explanation: Attribution embedded in prose is lost at the summarization step, because compression rewrites the prose. Claim-source mappings held as structured data can be merged and carried through synthesis intact.

why.B: Reconstructs attribution after the fact and invites confident mismatches, when the correct source was known upstream and discarded.
why.C: A prose instruction aimed at a compression step that is doing precisely what it was asked to do.
why.D: Length is not the mechanism; unstructured citations are lost at any output length.

stem: A reviewer returns your battery cost report with two objections. It presents $137/kWh and $89/kWh as a contradiction, when the first figure comes from a 2020 study and the second from a 2025 one. And where two 2025 sources genuinely disagree on installed capacity, 402 GW against 511 GW, the report silently states only the larger figure. Which two changes to the subagents' structured output contract address these? (Select 2)

options.text: Have the analysis subagent keep the value from the more highly cited of the two sources and discard the competing figure before it reaches synthesis.
Require every finding to carry its publication or collection date, so synthesis reads a difference over time as change rather than contradiction.
Have the analysis subagent return both conflicting values with their source attribution, leaving reconciliation to the coordinator.
Have the synthesis subagent average any conflicting figures and note the spread between them in a footnote to the report.

explanation: Undated findings make ordinary change over time look like a contradiction, and conflicts between credible sources are findings to annotate rather than disputes for an analysis agent to settle quietly.

why.A: Makes a reconciliation decision at the wrong layer and destroys the second value before the coordinator ever sees it.
why.D: Publishes a number that no source states, which is worse than reporting the disagreement.

stem: Your report generator applies one template to everything: each finding becomes a bullet in a flat list. A five-year quarterly revenue series arrives as 25 bullets that readers cannot compare, a regulatory news timeline becomes disconnected fragments with the sequence lost, and a benchmark comparison reads as unrelated sentences. Analysts say the reports are unusable for financial questions. What should change?

options.text: Generate a second, finance-specific version of the report from the same findings for the analyst audience.
Have the synthesis subagent omit any numeric series that does not fit the bullet template, on the grounds that such a series is unreadable in that form anyway.
Raise the character limit on each bullet so every figure has room for the context a reader needs around it.
Render each content type in its own form: financial series as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.

explanation: Flattening every content type into one uniform format destroys the structure that made each type readable. Synthesis output should preserve the shape appropriate to the content.

why.A: Duplicates output rather than fixing the rendering rule, and the news and technical content stay just as unreadable.
why.B: Discards the most valuable content in order to protect the template.
why.C: The defect is the form of the output, not the length of each item.
